output.summary: KEP-3744 proposes a process for updating supported Kubernetes release-1.x branches to build and release with new minor versions of Go, so patch releases use a supported Go version while preserving their stability and compatibility. Status is implementable, stage stable.
output.rationale: Kubernetes release branches historically stayed on one Go minor version, so the last months of each minor version's 14-month support window could lack Go security fixes. Go changes that break behavior made backporting risky, and the KEP's answer is a staged process: land prerequisite changes on the development branch, backport low-risk ones to release branches, and only then move release branches to the new Go minor version once conditions are met.

alternatives.option: Request the go team backport security fixes to more than two minor versions
alternatives.why_not: The percentage of patch releases containing security-related content has risen in recent years, so "security fixes only" would not necessarily mean fewer patch releases on older minor versions; not all security fixes can be cleanly backported.

alternatives.option: Maintain a custom patched version of older go minor versions with security fix backports
alternatives.why_not: It is not clear that all changes with security implications would be consistently noticed and backported, and staffing a fork would be an ongoing cost; a custom distribution also loses benefits of the standard widely tested distribution and could confuse security scanners.

evidence.quote: Because of this inconsistency, Kubernetes release branches historically remained on a single go minor version, and risked being unable to pick up go security fixes
Update release-1.x branches to build/release using go 1.N once all of these conditions are satisfied
Prioritize making the prereq changes as minimal and low-risk as possible. Merge those changes to the default Kubernetes development branch *prior* to updating to go 1.N.
go 1.N has been released at least 3 months
The primary drawback is risk of a user-facing regression in a patch release due to a go version change.
